full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'd treat this as the same result already reported, not a close variant.

**1. Model family.** This is a cellular automaton: a multi-state, outer-totalistic or priority-table rule on an aperiodic tiling. Cells are tiles, and neighbours are tiles that share at least a vertex. The tiling is the "spectre", the 2023 chiral monotile that needs no reflected copies. The companion tiling is the "hat", which does need reflections. The observed travelling objects are gliders.

**2. The specific behaviour.** A search for this exact setup turned up a paper whose abstract matches your observations closely. The paper is "Gliders on Aperiodic Monotilings: Cellular Automata on the Hat and Spectre". The abstract says:
- Evolutionary search discovers gliders on both monotilings. A sliding window regenerates the patch along the flight, and the gliders travel one million rings at constant speed and heading.
- All headings are quantized, to millidegrees, onto a six-spoke compass, which the abstract identifies as the fast axes of the tiling's graph metric.
- The search was extended to vertex neighborhoods and to priority-table rules whose non-quiescent states are visible to neighbors. Your four-rule priority list fits that description.
- Within edge-adjacency semi-totalistic rules, searches found only mortal travelers. Your rule uses vertex adjacency, which is consistent with that finding.

These match your 10⁶ rings, constant speed, six headings 60° apart with a tiny heading error, the regenerating window, and the hat/spectre pairing. The hat tiling is your "mirrored companion" family.

The source I could read is a catalogue entry (read.somethingorotherwhatever.com, "Interesting Esoterica", by James Edmond). It reproduces the abstract and lists an arXiv link, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22579v1. I could not open the full text. I therefore could not check the specific numbers (speed 0.5 rings per generation, 12 cells per traveller, 71% launch success) or whether your exact rule appears in it.

The catalogue entry says it was published in 2026, added 2026-10-14. The author names are not in the snippets I retrieved. The catalogue credits Edmond as the person who posted the entry, not necessarily as the paper's author. I have not verified the authors or whether the paper has appeared in a journal.

**Earlier background on gliders on aperiodic tilings.**
- Goucher, "Gliders in Cellular Automata on Penrose Tilings", Journal of Cellular Automata 7(5-6), 385–392, 2012. This is the earliest clear source. It presents the first glider capable of navigating an aperiodic tiling, in a four-state outer-totalistic automaton on generic tilings of quadrilaterals. It uses the vertex-sharing "generalised Moore" neighbourhood from Owens and Stepney, where neighbours are tiles sharing at least one vertex. Your rule has the same structure: four states and a quiescent background.
- Owens and Stepney, "Investigations of Game of Life cellular automata rules on Penrose tilings: lifetime and ash statistics", Automata 2008. It found no gliders on Penrose tilings, unlike cellular automata on regular tilings.
- Scholarpedia's "Cellular automata" article gives a short review. It notes that Goucher (2012) described a four-state automaton supporting gliders on aperiodic tilings. I could not find a better dedicated review.
- Goucher's paper itself notes that the glider's paths are a property of the Penrose geometry and not of the rule. That is consistent with the six-spoke heading quantisation in the hat/spectre paper.

**3. Citation check.** I checked titles and venues against the search results. Goucher 2012 (JCA 7(5-6), 385–392) is confirmed by the publisher page and the Scholarpedia entry. The 2026 hat/spectre paper is confirmed only through the catalogue entry and its abstract.

**4. Confidence: medium-high.** The abstract matches on tiling, behaviour, distance travelled and heading quantisation. The remaining uncertainty is that I could not read the paper's body or confirm the authors. I also could not confirm that your exact four-rule table, with states 0/1/3, appears in it.
